newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK--Tight ranges seen again.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK--Tight ranges seen again.

text.p: More range-bound trading was expected in the U.S. Treasuries market on Friday as anxious market players awaited critical data next week.

Existing home sales were set for release at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT and economists surveyed by Reuters expected, on average, that March sales would slip slightly to a 4.14 million annualized pace from 4.26 million in February.
But lacking an agreement on a balanced U.S. budget, prices were seen remaining in the same ranges they have been mired in all this week.

Tuesday will see the quarterly Employment Cost Index and nonfarm payrolls were to be reported next Friday. These will provide the most important readings on the strength of the U.S. labor market in weeks and will be key to whether the Federal Reserve votes to tighten monetary policy further at its May 20 meeting.

Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan has made it clear he would vote in favor of tightening if the economy hasn't slowed from the torrid pace seen in the fourth and first quarters even if no obvious signs of growing inflation had surfaced in official statistical reports.

Traders said continued heavy corporate issuance could weigh on the market on Friday and Monday, as pipelines remained full. Corporate issuers who needed to raise cash wanted to do so before the next tightening move was fully priced into the market, driving up their cost of funds.
"We'll see position squaring Friday and Monday because everyone's nervous about next week," said Brian Wesbury, chief economist at Griffin, Kubik, Stephens & Thompson Inc.
In addition to employment data, durable goods, personal income and consumption, NAPM, Chicago PMI, new home sales and leading economic indicators are were due for release.
Also on the data slate is preliminary first quarter GDP, which Wesbury expected to be at 4-1/4 percent -- though he said he had seen some estimates as high as 5.0 percent or more.
"The markets price in uncertainty and try to price in toward the worst case scenario. So the damage next week shouldn't be that great unless these numbers are really on the high side," Wesbury said.
Shocking numbers would be more than 300,000 in payrolls or a reading of 60 or higher for the NAPM.

"I've seen so little evidence of a slackening that I don't see the markets rallying ahead" of next week's data, said Mark Vitner, economist in the capital markets group at First Union Corp. However, he expected softer numbers may begin to appear in April data that will be reported in May.
"The ECI can upset this. It should show ... a sizable increase in wage costs and a pickup in strike activity," Vitner said.
Vitner said his group didn't expect to see yields on the long bond rise higher than 7-1/4 percent, however, as economic growth should start to slow.

Given the uncertainty ahead of next week's numbers traders said volume could be light on Friday. Maureen Mooney, senior analyst at GovPX, said a typical Friday saw volume of $60.8 billion by 1500 EDT/1900 GMT.

Late Thursday the benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury bond was trading 11/32 lower at 93-31/32 to yield 7.11 percent. The 10-year was at 95-09/32 to yield 6.92 percent; the five year at 99-06/32 to 6.82 percent and the two year at 99-23/32 to yield 6.53 percent.
